near_miss.lead: Reading a book versus gathering plants with cognate collect/read verbs.
near_miss.why_not: Norse lesa has bok as its object; Latvian lasa has zāles. The related verbs have different objects and contexts, and no second element establishes inherited phraseology.

near_miss.lead: Marriage negotiations involving son, daughter and wife.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse request for a wife and the Russian marriage fragment share ordinary kinship words; Greek partners concern other family situations. No distinctive shared syntactic formula survives, and the Russian fragment is too damaged to strengthen the case.

near_miss.lead: Seen or heard as the basis of testimony.
near_miss.why_not: Norse seet eða hǫyrt is a real legal pairing, but the slab partner is Ariadne’s unheard complaint, not witness testimony. Searches for the Norse seeing/hearing roots returned ordinary Norse perception pairings; Sanskrit dṛś + śru returned numerous seen/heard pairings, including MBh 1.46.s65 and s85, but with neither verb cognate to this Norse pair. No inherited equation is established.

near_miss.lead: Red blood falling in battle verse.
near_miss.why_not: Norse bloð fell rautt is coherent battle language, but neither slab partner mentions blood. Red-root and blood-form searches found Homer Il. 11.394, where blood reddens earth, and medical descriptions of red blood. Only the color root matches the Homeric passage; the noun and syntax differ. Natural blood color alone cannot establish inheritance.

near_miss.lead: Kinship lists and paired father/mother wording.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse text is a sequence of named genealogical relationships. Partners concern famine, marriage guardianship, prohibited or commanded kin relations, and heroic parentage. Several kinship nouns are cognate, but they do not form the same distinctive figure. Herodotus 1.137.2 is relevant to the separately considered kin-killing lead, not to this genealogy.

near_miss.lead: Trust in one’s might and main; blessing a drinking cup.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse might/main doublet and ritual cup are worth close reading, but the Greek partner has collective wailing and groaning after naval defeat. Þór versus στόνος is a root-level retrieval connection, not shared ritual wording; no matching collocation appears in the anchors.

near_miss.lead: Drawing/pouring water with cognate ausa and ἀφύσσω.
near_miss.why_not: This is the clearest two-root lexical match: Norse vatn and Greek ὕδωρ with related liquid-handling verbs. But the Norse water is instrumental in sprinkling and naming a child, whereas Homer has accusative water as a ship’s provision. A search of ἀφύσσω also finds ordinary wine drawing and libations. Neither a distinctive shared ritual nor the same syntactic relation supports inherited phraseology.

near_miss.lead: Killing father, mother and sister as an enumeration of grave offences.
near_miss.why_not: Norse drepr governs a longer disjunctive list, while AVP 19.46.s26 repeats -hā in mother/father/sister-killer compounds. The kinship terms are cognate, but the killing verb, order, syntax and list boundaries differ. Greek Herodotus 1.137.2 adds father/mother killing but not the sister. Searching mātṛ + pitṛ + han found this AVP witness and MBh 12.258.s19 and 12.259.s24, with different ethical arguments. Close-kin killing is independently taboo; the passages do not establish a distinctive inherited list.
